meta.regime: The regime is still policy differentials against a weakening dollar, but the energy leg underneath it has flipped direction and that reprices several trades. For two sessions this book carried the view that crude was fading and quietly disarming the hawks everywhere. That was wrong, and the correction is the most important thing on the page. Crude rose more than 5% last week and holds above 82 this morning - WTI 82.09, Brent 88.55 - because US Treasury Secretary Bessent said Washington would impose unprecedented economic measures while MAINTAINING the naval blockade of Iranian ports, because the IEA is now forecasting the widest global supply shortfall of 2026 in five years, because Houthi militants hit Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery, and because Israel struck Lebanon over the weekend, killing 11 people including a senior Hezbollah commander. The interim US-Iran ceasefire agreement formally expires today and Trump is preparing new sanctions aimed at forcing Iran to capitulate. Iran and Oman have agreed shipping-lane coordinates but not a reopening, and Tehran's position has not moved: no reopening while the blockade stands. What caps the price is that Middle Eastern producers are covertly moving millions of barrels through the waterway anyway. The dollar side of the regime is unchanged and still working - DXY 99.50 and lower again today, EUR/USD 1.1586 at a fresh two-month high, GBP/USD 1.3554, AUD/USD 0.7106, NZD/USD 0.5913 at a 2.5-month high, USD/CHF 0.8114 - because nothing has undone the four-print US deterioration and September hike odds sit near 33%. The overnight event was Japan, where Q2 GDP missed hard at 0.3% q/q and 1.1% annualised against 0.5% and 2.0% expected, with flat private consumption and a sharp capex contraction, and yet the yen firmed to 159.07 and the 10-year JGB printed 2.93%, a multi-decade high, with roughly 62% priced for a September 18 hike. A weak GDP print that does not move the rate market is a market telling you the BoJ is going anyway.

dailyRead: Start with the correction, because it is the day's real news and it moves positions. This book spent Friday and the weekend describing an oil market that was fading - WTI at 80.96, a reopening being priced, the Canadian terms-of-trade leg thinning, cheap energy quietly removing the hawks' best argument everywhere. That framing is wrong and today it gets reversed. Crude gained more than 5% last week and holds above 82 this morning: WTI 82.09, Brent 88.55. The drivers are specific. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington would impose unprecedented economic measures on Iran while MAINTAINING the naval blockade of its ports, with more announcements due this week. The International Energy Agency is now forecasting the widest global supply shortfall of 2026 in five years, on top of the July stock draw of 2.2 million barrels a day that took total inventories below 7.9 billion barrels. Iran-backed Houthi militants struck Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery. Over the weekend Israel launched fresh strikes on Lebanon, killing 11 people including a senior Hezbollah commander. And the interim US-Iran ceasefire agreement - the one signed on June 17 for 60 days - FORMALLY EXPIRES TODAY, with President Trump preparing a new sanctions package designed to force Iranian capitulation and negotiations to reopen the strait deadlocked. Iran and Oman have agreed the geographical coordinates of a proposed corridor, inbound through Iranian waters in the north and outbound through Omani waters in the south, plus a joint coordination centre - but Tehran's foreign ministry has not shifted an inch on the condition: as long as the US naval blockade continues, the conditions for reopening do not exist. The only thing keeping a lid on price is that Middle Eastern producers are covertly moving millions of barrels through the waterway with tankers switching off transponders, and that US forces are increasing their ability to escort vessels. Three consequences follow directly. USOIL flips from RANGE to LONG. Canada gets its terms-of-trade leg back and moves above sterling in the ranking, with money markets now pricing roughly 13bp of BoC tightening by year-end, about a 52% chance of a hike, which is a materially more hawkish path than the flat hold I carried yesterday. And GER40 loses the cheap-input tailwind that was half its long thesis, so it goes to LOW-MED. The dollar leg of the regime, by contrast, is entirely intact and still paying. The dollar index is at 99.50 and lower again today, EUR/USD printed a fresh two-month high at 1.1586, GBP/USD is 1.3554, AUD/USD 0.7106, NZD/USD 0.5913 at a two-and-a-half-month high, USD/CHF 0.8114 and USD/CAD 1.3862. Nothing has undone the sequence - July payrolls CONTRACTING 23,000 with 146,000 of downward revisions, CPI 3.4% headline and 2.5% core, PPI 4.7% against 5.0% expected, retail sales -0.6% m/m with the control group at -0.4%, Michigan sentiment at 51.0 - and September hold odds sit near 67%. Wednesday's FOMC minutes cover the July 29 meeting where Logan, Hammack and Kashkari all dissented FOR a hike, but Newsquawk's own framing is right: the minutes are backward-looking and the market will probably look through them, because everything decisive has printed since. Jackson Hole on August 27 remains the dollar's real event, and note the asymmetry that today's oil move creates - a Warsh who wants to keep a hike alive now has a live energy argument again that he did not have on Friday. USD holds at -2 WEAKENING but that is the one thread to watch. The overnight event was Japan and it resolved in an instructive way. Preliminary Q2 GDP rose just 0.3% q/q against a 0.5% consensus, and 1.1% annualised against 2.0%, with flat private consumption and a sharp contraction in business investment - a genuinely poor print that on its face gives the Bank an excuse to wait until October. The market did not take it. USD/JPY firmed to 159.07, down 0.16%, and the 10-year JGB is at 2.93%, a multi-decade high, with roughly 62% priced for a hike to 1.25% on September 18. The reason is the July Summary of Opinions, which was more hawkish than anything the Bank has published in this cycle: members explicitly named Middle East developments, expanding AI-related demand and a weak yen as forces pushing inflation up, one said inflation risks are skewed sharply to the upside as higher oil costs feed through, another said the pace of hikes could EXCEED market expectations, and another said the cost of delaying a hike is not insignificant. Set that against PPI at 7.2% with import prices up 29.1% y/y, Tokyo CPI at 2.0% and Tokyo core 1.9%, wages at 3.4% with real earnings positive for a sixth month, and inflation expectations at 2.7%. Rising oil makes all of this worse for Japan, not better - the trade balance is already -JPY 407bn, the current account swung to -JPY 923bn and terms of trade have deteriorated to 81.62. JPY stays -1 MIXED: the policy tail into September 18 is real, 160 is where the MoF has already acted once, but carry keeps winning the tape. Friday's July national CPI, with core expected at 1.8% from 1.6%, is the decider. The euro keeps the top score at +2 and today its case actually improved. July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5% and services at 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, deposit facility 2.25% re-verified on TE this morning against the 2.40% refi headline, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3%, composite PMI 52.0, ZEW 23.4. The reason today is better than Friday is that euro-area energy inflation was already accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5% and Lagarde's second-round-effects framing was the ECB's stated reason to keep hiking - a framing that was losing force at falling crude and regains it at Brent 88.55. September 10 stays around 70% priced. The standing caution is unchanged: TE describes the post-July tone as wait-and-see, consumer inflation expectations fell to 3.0% from 3.5% and producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y. Australia holds +2 and the RBA press conference is the anchor. Bullock revealed the Board did NOT discuss a cut at the August 11 meeting - only whether to raise or hold - said it was thinking hard about when it might be appropriate to raise rates and that another hike was possible, and the SoMP still has underlying inflation at 3.3% by end-2026 with no midpoint return until late 2027 and risks skewed UP. The cash rate at 4.35% is the highest in the G10. Chinese activity data came and went this morning without damaging the commodity bloc: Shanghai closed up 0.98%, copper JUMPED 1.72% to 6.71 on supply concerns rather than falling on demand, and AUD gained 0.33%. Thursday's July labour report, expected around +20-25k after June's +76,343, is the real Aussie risk. Canada moves to third. July employment rose 75,100, the largest in two years, unemployment fell to a two-year low of 6.4% and participation rose to 65.1%; CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% are both below target, which is what keeps the BoC at 2.25% on a sixth hold - but with crude back above 82 the energy-driven upside risk the Bank named is live again, the loonie has now gained for a third straight week and Canadian yields rose on strong macro data. July CPI at 12:30Z today is the immediate input and it cuts both ways. Sterling stays +1 but the hawkish case is drifting. Q2 GDP was +0.4% q/q with the y/y rate accelerating to 1.2% from 0.9%, unemployment 4.9%, wages 4.3% including bonuses, and the July 30 decision was a 6-3 hold with three dissenters - but Newsquawk's read of the GDP detail is that the June breakdown was weak, the May series was revised down, pharmaceuticals drove volatile manufacturing strength, and the whole thing works in favour of the doves who spoke at the last meeting. The June trade deficit at GBP 5.54bn and RICS at -30 sit underneath. Tuesday's labour report at 06:00Z and Wednesday's CPI at 06:00Z decide it, and note July UK headline CPI will likely RISE on the Ofgem cap adjustment, which is a mechanical hawkish print rather than a real one. GBP/NZD comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM on that. Switzerland stays 0 MIXED, but the escalation risk changes how the crosses should be sized. Policy rate 0.00%, CPI 0.4%, core 0.3%, PPI -2.1%, unemployment 3.0% - a funding currency on the numbers - against the Q2 GDP shock at +1.5% q/q (pharma-distorted), services PMI 63.9 and ZEW +10. With a ceasefire expiring today and strikes in Lebanon over the weekend, the haven bid is a live upside risk to the franc, so EUR/CHF and AUD/CHF come down to LOW-MED while USD/CHF stays a MEDIUM short because both legs work. CHF/JPY goes UP to MEDIUM: a haven franc against a yen whose import bill just got worse. New Zealand remains the cleanest fundamental short at -2 and nothing changed - Q3 two-year business inflation expectations at 2.34% against a 2.7% forecast, unemployment 5.6% and the highest since 2015, wage growth 2.1%, ANZ commodity prices +0.5% y/y, GDT +0.1% - but the kiwi just made a 2.5-month high at 0.5913 on pure dollar weakness for the second session running. NZD/USD stays RANGE. Trade the short where the differential is unambiguous: EUR/NZD, AUD/NZD, NZD/CAD and NZD/CHF. Finally the metals, which all confirmed the same regime this morning: gold 4,392 up 0.39% and pressing toward its highs on a weak dollar plus a live geopolitical tail, silver 65.72 up 1.64%, copper 6.71 up 1.72% on supply concerns. XAU/USD goes to HIGH conviction, and XAG and XCU both upgrade to MEDIUM - yesterday's worry that a Chinese demand miss would drag the industrial leg simply did not materialise.

USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike - Logan, Hammack and Kashkari - and Chair Warsh again declined to offer forward guidance, which is why analysts now treat every meeting as live. Re-verified on TE this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% from 3.5%, core 2.5% from 2.6% and a five-month low, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised, GDP annual 2.1%, unemployment 4.1%, participation at a five-year-low 61.4%, initial claims 209,000, retail sales -0.6% m/m, Michigan sentiment 51.0. The four-print deterioration is intact: payrolls CONTRACTED 23,000 in July with the prior two months revised down a combined 146,000 and average hourly earnings at 3.2% y/y; PPI final demand 4.7% against 5.0% expected with the monthly index flat; and July retail sales fell 0.6% against +0.1% expected with the Control Group at -0.4% against +0.3% expected, the component that feeds GDP directly. Money markets price roughly a 67% chance of a September hold. Wednesday's FOMC minutes at 18:00Z will show how far the hawkish sentiment extended beyond the three dissenters and what weight the Committee put on supply shocks and the AI investment boom entrenching inflation - but they cover a meeting held before CPI, PPI, payrolls and retail sales all landed soft, so the market will likely look through them. The genuine risk to the dollar short is not the minutes, it is oil: crude is back above 82 and Brent at 88.55, which hands Warsh a live energy argument at Jackson Hole on Aug 27 that he did not have on Friday. July core PCE lands Aug 26, tracking 0.16-0.23% m/m.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (~70% priced, and the energy case just improved)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, main refinancing 2.40% and marginal lending 2.65%, confirmed unchanged on Jul 23 and re-verified on TE this morning - use the 2.25% depo, not the 2.40% headline. The domestic case is unchanged and self-supporting: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4% and services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q accelerating from flat in Q1 and +1.0% y/y from a revised 0.5%, with Spain +0.7%, Netherlands +0.4%, France back to +0.2% and Germany and Italy both +0.2%. Final composite PMI 52.0, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3% and stable, ZEW 23.4 from 9.5, capacity utilisation 78.5. What is BETTER today than on Friday is the energy leg. Euro-area energy inflation accelerated to 10.0% from 8.5% in the July HICP, and Lagarde's stated justification for continuing to tighten was that the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they drive broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects. That argument was weakening at falling crude; with Brent back at 88.55 and the US-Iran ceasefire expiring, it regains force. EUR/USD is 1.1586, a fresh two-month high above Friday's break of the 100-DMA at 1.1566. The standing caution stands: TE characterises the ECB's post-July stance as explicit wait-and-see, euro-area consumer inflation expectations fell to 3.0% from 3.5%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y with the monthly index at -0.3%, food inflation is 1.2% and June retail sales were -0.3% m/m. EZ final July CPI lands Wednesday and August flash PMIs Friday, with manufacturing expected at 52.0 from 51.9.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; the hawkish case is drifting)
GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus, verified on TE today, with TE's end-of-quarter model still at 4.00%. The headline data remains good: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q against +0.3% expected with the y/y rate ACCELERATING to 1.2% from 0.9% and beating the 1.1% consensus, June monthly GDP +0.3% against an expected decline, unemployment 4.9% with 1.76 million unemployed, wages 4.3% including bonuses and 3.4% excluding, real pay positive at 1.3%, employment +148,000 from +99,000, June CPI 2.6% headline and 2.6% core with services at 3.6%. But the read underneath has softened. Newsquawk's assessment of the GDP release is that while it beat, the June breakdown was weaker than expected, the May series was revised DOWN, and volatile pharmaceuticals drove the manufacturing strength - and that on balance it works in favour of the members who made dovish arguments at the last meeting rather than the three dissenters. On wages, the components continue to show a moderation in the rate of growth once public-sector awards are stripped out. The unresolved negatives are real: the June trade deficit widened to GBP 5.54bn from 1.04bn against a 3.6bn forecast, the RICS house price balance is -30, vacancies are 712,000 and below pre-pandemic, inactivity is rising to 9.11 million at a 20.9% rate. GBP/USD is 1.3554 on the dollar leg, not the sterling one. Two decisive prints this week: the labour report Tuesday at 06:00Z, and July CPI Wednesday at 06:00Z where the headline will likely RISE mechanically on the Ofgem utility cap adjustment even as PMI price gauges pointed to cooling - a hawkish-looking print that is not really hawkish.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (~62% priced - and a bad GDP print did not shift it)
JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%, verified on TE. This morning's preliminary Q2 GDP was a clear miss - 0.3% q/q against 0.5% expected and 1.1% annualised against 2.0% - with flat private consumption and a sharp contraction in business investment, a print that on its own would justify waiting until October. The market refused it. USD/JPY firmed to 159.07, down 0.16%, and the 10-year JGB yield is 2.93% after printing 2.88% Friday, a multi-decade high, with money markets holding roughly 62% for a hike to 1.25% on September 18. The reason is the July Summary of Opinions, which was the most hawkish document of this cycle: one member said Middle East developments, expanding AI-related demand and a weak yen all work to push inflation up; another said inflation risks are skewed sharply to the upside as higher oil costs feed into consumer prices; another said the pace of BoJ rate hikes could EXCEED market expectations; and another said the cost of delaying a hike is not insignificant. Reuters has separately reported that the record joint Japan-US intervention and Treasury Secretary Bessent's stated preference for an early Japanese move have all but locked September. The domestic case is the best in three decades: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y with base pay at 3.4%, real earnings including bonuses +1.6% and positive for a sixth month; June CPI 1.7% from 1.5% with core 1.6% and core-core 1.7%; Tokyo July CPI 2.0% from 1.7%, Tokyo core 1.9% from 1.6%, Tokyo ex food and energy 2.0%; PPI 7.2% y/y with import prices +29.1%; inflation expectations 2.7% from 2.4%. Today's rise in crude makes the structural weakness worse, not better - trade balance -JPY 407bn, current account -JPY 923bn from +3,968bn, terms of trade 81.62 from 82.71. Unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18. Friday's July national CPI at 23:30Z Thursday, with core expected at 1.8% from 1.6%, is the decider; the trade balance lands Thursday.

AUD.note: Held the cash rate at 4.35% on Aug 11 in a UNANIMOUS decision as all 37 Reuters economists expected, verified on TE today, and the press conference did more work than the statement. Governor Bullock revealed the Board did NOT discuss a rate cut at all - the only question on the table was whether to raise or to hold - said the Board hopes to slow the economy, sees upside risks to inflation, is thinking hard about when it might be appropriate to raise rates, and that it was possible another hike would be needed. The statement retained the option of increasing the cash rate target further if upside risks materialise. The August Statement on Monetary Policy remains the anchor: underlying inflation at 3.3% by end-2026 and no return to around the midpoint of the 2-3% band until late 2027, with risks to that projection skewed UP. TE's model carries 4.60%. The honest offset is that the release was read as marginally LESS hawkish than previous ones - the Bank trimmed some CPI forecasts in the SoMP, said financial conditions now appear somewhat restrictive after three hikes this year, and expects the economy to return to balance in 2027, a little earlier than previously forecast. Q2 detail still supports the hawks: headline CPI cooled to 3.8% from 4.0% and trimmed mean rose to 3.6% from 3.5%, but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%. Labour: employment +76,343, unemployment 4.4%, participation 67.0%. July PMIs services 53.6, composite 53.2, manufacturing 52.0; consumer confidence 83.9; commodity prices +15.4% y/y. Chinese activity data this morning did not damage the Aussie - Shanghai closed +0.98%, copper rose 1.72% on supply concerns and AUD/USD gained 0.33% to 0.7106. Thursday's July labour report at 01:30Z is the live risk: consensus is +20-25k after +76.3k with unemployment at 4.4-4.5%, and Westpac notes underlying jobs growth has slowed to a 1.1% annualised three-month pace.

NZD.when: Sept 2 (the hike is off; the survey settled it)
NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, verified on TE, and that cycle is over. The RBNZ quarterly survey was the confirmation and it missed badly: Q3 two-year business inflation expectations came in at 2.34% against a 2.7% FORECAST and 2.53% prior, the lowest since Q4 2025, with one-year expectations collapsing to 2.60% from 3.41%, one of the largest single-quarter falls in the series; only the five- and ten-year tails ticked up, to 2.31% and 2.20%. The risk this book flagged against the kiwi short was a JUMP in expectations forcing a rethink, and it went decisively the other way. The labour side is the worst in the G10: Q2 unemployment 5.6% against 5.4% expected and the highest since Q3 2015, unemployed persons 171,000, wage growth just 2.1% y/y, employment +0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%, youth unemployment 17.2%. Headline CPI is 4.1% and above the 1-3% band but 27.5% of it was petrol, core is 3.2%. The domestic-sentiment offset is genuine - July ANZ business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, consumer confidence 99.3, manufacturing PMI 59.7, composite 53.6 - but ANZ commodity prices decelerated to +0.5% y/y from +2.7% and the Global Dairy Trade index rose only 0.1%, so the terms-of-trade support is gone. The caveat is now two sessions old and hardening: NZD/USD is 0.5913, a two-and-a-half-month high, made entirely on dollar weakness rather than anything domestic. That is why NZD/USD stays RANGE and the short is expressed against EUR, AUD, CAD and CHF. One thing to watch: rising crude is a direct negative for New Zealand's terms of trade and would push that 27.5% petrol contribution back up, which is a hawkish tail for Q3 CPI but not for the September 2 meeting.

CAD.when: Sept 2 (but ~52% of a hike is priced by year-end)
CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, re-verified on TE this morning, with the Bank noting the economy was adjusting to recent shocks and that energy-driven inflation pressures were easing. That last clause is what changed over the weekend. Crude is back above 82 with Brent at 88.55 after a 5% weekly gain, so the energy-driven upside risk the BoC named is live again rather than easing, and the terms-of-trade thinning I flagged on Friday reverses. The Canadian dollar has now gained for a THIRD straight week and Canadian yields rose on strong macroeconomic data. Money markets price roughly 13bp of tightening by year-end, equivalent to about a 52% chance of a 25bp hike - a meaningfully more hawkish path than a flat hold, and worth noting the policy rate sits near the LOWER end of the Bank's estimated neutral range, so further cuts would move policy into accommodative territory. Rabobank still expects a hold through year-end. catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz - blockade, sanctions and the Iran/Oman corridor
catalysts.note: Iran and Oman have agreed corridor coordinates and a joint coordination centre, but Tehran will not reopen while the US naval blockade stands, and Bessent has promised unprecedented measures while keeping it. Producers are moving barrels covertly with transponders off.

USD/JPY is 159.07 after a weak Q2 GDP print failed to push it higher. The MoF has already demonstrated at this level that it will act, and Bessent has said Japan should reinforce intervention with supporting policy.

geopolitics: The correction to make today is that the oil market did not fade - it rallied, and the reopening trade that was being priced last week has been taken back out. Crude gained more than 5% over the week and holds above 82 this morning, with WTI at 82.09 and Brent at 88.55. Five things drove it. First, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington would impose UNPRECEDENTED economic measures on Iran while MAINTAINING the naval blockade of Iranian ports, with further announcements expected this week - the opposite of the de-escalation the price had started to assume. Second, the International Energy Agency is now forecasting the widest global supply shortfall of 2026 in five years, layered on top of its Aug 12 report that inventories fell 2.2 million barrels a day in July to below 7.9 billion barrels for the first time since early 2025. Third, Iran-backed Houthi militants struck Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery in the Red Sea. Fourth, Israel launched fresh strikes on Lebanon over the weekend, killing 11 people including a senior Hezbollah commander. And fifth, the interim US-Iran ceasefire agreement signed by Trump and Pezeshkian on June 17 for a 60-day term FORMALLY EXPIRES TODAY, with Trump preparing a new sanctions package aimed at forcing Iranian capitulation and negotiations to end the conflict deadlocked. On the diplomatic track, Iran and Oman have agreed the geographical coordinates of a proposed corridor - inbound traffic through a northern lane in Iranian territorial waters, outbound through a southern lane in Omani waters, plus a joint coordination centre to manage traffic - which is a real departure from the decades-old arrangement where everything ran through Omani waters. But the US is not a party to those talks, and Iran's foreign ministry has not moved on the condition: as long as the US naval blockade continues, the conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz do not exist, and national security chief Zolghadr's list still runs to lifting the blockade, withdrawing forces, permanently ending the war, compensation and unfreezing assets. What is capping the price rather than resolving it is physical: Middle Eastern producers are covertly moving millions of barrels through the waterway with some tankers switching off transponders, and US officials say American forces are increasing their capacity to escort vessels, so the effective throughput is higher than the official picture even though the strait is nominally closed. The FX read has four parts and three of them changed today. First and most direct, Canada gets its terms-of-trade leg back: crude above 82 revives exactly the energy-driven inflation pressure the BoC described as EASING in July, which is why markets now price roughly 13bp of tightening by year-end and why CAD moves above GBP in the ranking. Second, the euro's hawkish case improves rather than decays - euro-area energy HICP was already accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, and Lagarde's second-round-effects justification for continuing to tighten needs elevated energy to stay credible into Sept 10. Third, Japan gets worse: the trade balance is already -JPY 407bn, the current account swung to -JPY 923bn from +3,968bn, terms of trade have fallen to 81.62, and yen-based import prices are up 29.1% y/y - a rising oil price transmits into Japanese inflation and Japanese weakness simultaneously, which is precisely the tension the BoJ's July Summary of Opinions described. Fourth, and this is the risk-management point, the franc's haven bid stops being theoretical on the day a ceasefire expires: EUR/CHF and AUD/CHF come down to LOW-MED because an escalation squeezes every CHF-short cross in the book at once, while NZD/CHF and USD/CHF are the two where escalation actually helps. Note finally the second-order effect on the US: the Michigan sentiment collapse to 51.0 explicitly cited Middle East-driven prices, so the energy shock is already reaching American household expectations, and a Fed chair looking for a reason to keep a September hike alive at Jackson Hole on Aug 27 now has one he did not have on Friday.
